query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high‐temperature structural and chemical stability of HEA nanoparticles is maintained by an entropy‐driven stabilization mechanism. Specifically, the high configurational entropy in equimolar multi‐metal nanoparticles produces significant lattice distortions and high diffusion barriers (sluggish kinetics) that prevent phase separation and elemental segregation, even under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions from 473 to 1923 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios arranged as a single-phase solid solution (e.g., FCC or BCC) with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Thermal exposure and cycling under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions spanning temperatures from 473 K up to 1923 K.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in controlled atmospheres (oxidizing/reducing as appropriate) with identical supports and baseline synthesis protocols, ensuring that only the thermal energy and operating environment are varied between tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortions and the high configurational entropy that lead to sluggish atomic diffusion and high energy barriers for atom mobility.
generation.mechanism: At the elevated temperatures relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric applications, the enhanced thermal energy that would normally drive atomic diffusion and phase separation is counterbalanced by the kinetic barriers imposed by lattice distortions. This slows down atomic rearrangements, thereby preserving the uniform single-phase solid solution despite the thermodynamic impetus toward segregation. In contrast, systems with lower configurational entropy (or less lattice distortion) would have faster diffusion rates and are more prone to phase decomposition.
generation.predicted_outcome: After thermal treatment across the 473–1923 K range, the HEA nanoparticles will retain their single-phase structure and uniform elemental distribution as evidenced by minimal shifts in lattice parameters and the absence of phase segregation or agglomeration compared to their initial state.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles characterized by a consistent, homogeneous solid solution structure before any high-temperature treatment.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism should hold provided that the alloy maintains near-equimolar ratios and that external factors (e.g., catalytic supports, reactive atmospheres) do not independently drive rapid diffusion or promote phase transformations. If temperatures far exceed 1923 K or if severe surface effects are induced by the environment, the entropy stabilization may be overcome.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of support interactions, surface oxidation, and possible minor intermetallic formation under specific reactive conditions are not fully quantified. Additionally, the precise temperature at which the kinetic barriers may fail is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set of high-entropy (equimolar five-or-more metal) nanoparticles and a control set (e.g., bimetallic or lower-entropy nanoparticles). Subject both sets to identical thermal cycling and exposure within the operating range (473–1923 K) under representative catalytic/thermoelectric atmospheres. After treatment, analyze the phase stability, grain size, and elemental distribution using high-resolution XRD, TEM, and STEM-EDS.
measurements: Phase identification and lattice parameter determination using X-ray diffraction and electron diffraction
Elemental mapping and chemical homogeneity assessment via STEM-EDS
Grain size and morphology evaluation using high-resolution TEM
Diffusion behavior (if feasible) via tracer or in situ annealing studies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoparticles exhibit significant phase separation, elemental segregation, or grain coarsening—comparable to or exceeding that observed in the lower-entropy control samples—under the same thermal conditions, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy and lattice distortion provide the kinetic stabilization would be refuted.

The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).
